aliases: law of the internet user experience
shortDef: People expect your product to work like the others they use.
longDef: Users spend most of their time in other products, so their expectations are formed elsewhere. Matching established conventions means their existing knowledge transfers and they can start using yours immediately. Novelty is not free — every deviation from convention has to earn back the cost of relearning.
example: A shopping cart icon in the top right, and a logo that returns to the homepage, work because a thousand other sites taught them.
misuse: It is not an argument that you can never innovate. It says deviation must be worth its price, not that it is forbidden.

shortDef: The more choices you show, the longer the decision takes.
longDef: Decision time grows with the number and complexity of the options presented. The practical response is not always fewer features but fewer things visible at once: group, prioritise and defer. It applies to considered choices, not to scanning a familiar list where people already know what they want.
example: A signup screen offering three plans converts faster than one offering eleven, even when the eleven include the three.
misuse: Not a mandate to strip everything back. A long alphabetical list of countries is fine, because nobody is comparing them.

shortDef: Targets that are bigger and closer are faster to hit.
longDef: The time to reach a target depends on its size and its distance from where the pointer already is. It is the reason primary actions are large, the reason screen edges are valuable, and the reason a 20-pixel close button is a bad idea on a phone. On touch devices the finger, not the cursor, sets the minimum.
example: The macOS menu bar is fast because the screen edge stops the pointer — the target is effectively infinitely tall.
misuse: Making a destructive button huge is Fitts's Law working against you. Speed is not always the goal.

shortDef: People hold about seven items in working memory at once.
longDef: The original finding concerns immediate memory span, and later work puts the practical figure closer to four. The useful takeaway is not a magic number of menu items but that working memory is small, so interfaces should chunk information and avoid requiring people to carry values from screen to screen.
example: Phone numbers are grouped in threes and fours because eleven separate digits exceed what most people can hold.
misuse: Widely misquoted as "never show more than seven options". Miller was describing memory, not navigation.

shortDef: Every process has complexity that cannot be removed, only moved.
longDef: Some complexity is inherent to the problem, and the only question is who absorbs it: the user, the designer or the engineer. Good products push it toward the system — smart defaults, inference, sensible fallbacks — rather than exposing it as another field on a form. Pretending it can be deleted just relocates it somewhere worse.
example: An email client that parses "lunch Thursday 1pm" absorbs the complexity of date entry instead of showing three dropdowns.
misuse: Not an excuse for a complicated interface. The law says complexity must be handled, not displayed.

shortDef: Below about 400ms response, attention holds and productivity rises.
longDef: When a system responds faster than roughly four hundred milliseconds, people stay in the loop rather than waiting on it, and their pace increases sharply. Above it, attention wanders and the session slows disproportionately. It is why perceived performance work — optimistic updates, skeletons, prefetching — pays back more than it costs.
example: Search that filters as you type keeps you engaged; the same search behind a submit button and a two-second wait does not.
misuse: Adding a spinner does not meet the threshold. It acknowledges the wait rather than removing it.

shortDef: People judge an experience by its peak and its ending.
longDef: Memory of an experience is dominated by its most intense moment and by how it finished, not by the average or the duration. That makes the last screen of a flow disproportionately important, and it makes one bad moment expensive even in an otherwise smooth journey. Design the ending deliberately rather than letting it be whatever is left.
example: A ride-hailing app ending on a clean receipt and a driver thank-you leaves a better memory than the same trip ending on a survey.
misuse: It does not license a painful middle. A high peak of frustration is exactly what gets remembered.

shortDef: People remember the first and last items in a list best.
longDef: Items at the start benefit from primacy and items at the end from recency, while the middle is where things go to be forgotten. It argues for placing the most important actions at the two ends of a navigation set. It also explains why a critical option buried mid-menu goes unused.
example: Mobile tab bars put the primary destination first and the account last, leaving lower-traffic sections in the middle.

shortDef: The item that differs from its neighbours is the one remembered.
longDef: When several similar things sit together, the odd one out gets attention and is recalled better. It is the mechanism behind a single filled primary button among outlined ones, or one highlighted pricing tier. Its power is finite: emphasise two things and you have emphasised nothing.
example: A pricing table where only the middle plan has a border and a label pulls most of the clicks to that plan.
misuse: Difference must not be carried by colour alone, or the effect disappears for anyone who cannot distinguish it.

shortDef: Unfinished tasks stay in mind more than completed ones.
longDef: An interrupted or incomplete task keeps a foothold in memory until it is resolved. Progress indicators, partially filled profiles and unfinished checklists all exploit this, creating a mild pull back to the product. Used heavily it becomes a nag, and people resolve the tension by leaving.
example: A profile showing "60% complete" draws people back to fill in the remaining fields more than a plain edit link does.
misuse: Not a licence for permanent unread badges. Manufactured incompleteness reads as pressure, not as helpfulness.

shortDef: People perceive attractive designs as easier to use.
longDef: A polished interface is judged more usable than a plain one, even when both perform identically, and users forgive more of its small problems. That is genuinely valuable, and it is also a trap in research: a beautiful prototype can mask usability problems that only surface once it ships. Watch behaviour, not praise.
example: Participants rate a well-typeset form as simpler than an unstyled one, while taking the same time to complete both.
misuse: It does not mean visual polish substitutes for usability. It means polish hides the evidence.

shortDef: Effort increases as a visible goal gets closer.
longDef: People speed up the nearer they are to finishing, which makes visible progress a powerful completion aid. Starting someone partway along — two stamps already on the loyalty card — triggers the same acceleration. The progress shown has to be real, or the trust cost outweighs the completion gain.
example: A four-step checkout that marks step one complete on arrival sees fewer drop-offs than one starting at zero.

shortDef: Work expands to fill the time available for it.
longDef: Given a generous deadline, a task consumes the whole of it. In interface terms, if a process is allowed to feel long, users will settle into that pace and expect it. Constraining the time — through defaults, autofill and shorter forms — often improves both speed and satisfaction.
example: A tax form that pre-fills known data is finished faster, and users report it as less onerous, than the same form left blank.

shortDef: Accept input liberally, produce output conservatively.
longDef: Borrowed from network protocol design, it argues that a system should tolerate whatever form the input arrives in and be strict about what it emits. For interfaces this means accepting a phone number with or without spaces, and a date in whatever order the person typed it, rather than rejecting it. The strictness belongs in your own output, not in the demands you make of people.
example: A card field that silently strips spaces and dashes instead of showing "invalid card number".
misuse: Being liberal is not the same as being silent. Show what you understood the input to mean.

shortDef: Prefer the simplest option that still does the job.
longDef: Among designs that meet the requirement, the one with the fewest parts is usually the best bet: fewer states to build, fewer things to explain, fewer ways to break. It is a tie-breaker rather than a design method — it applies once the options all work. The trap is treating "fewest elements on screen" as the goal instead of "fewest necessary".
example: Choosing a single text field with inline validation over a wizard, when both collect the same three values.
misuse: Simplicity for its own sake produces hidden functionality and mystery-meat icons. Removing labels is not simplification.

shortDef: People start using software immediately rather than reading instructions.
longDef: Users skip the manual and the tour because they want to get something done now, even though reading would be faster overall. Designing around it means putting help where the difficulty happens rather than up front, and making the first attempt recoverable. Onboarding that must be read to be survived will not be read.
example: A tooltip that appears the first time someone opens the filter panel beats a five-screen tour shown at signup.
misuse: The answer is not more forced tutorials. It is an interface that can be learned by trying.

shortDef: Things placed close together are perceived as related.
longDef: Spacing communicates grouping before any border or colour does, and it does so faster than reading. Getting proximity wrong is the single most common cause of confusing forms: a label sitting equidistant between two fields belongs to neither. Space is the cheapest grouping tool available.
example: A label 4px above its input and 20px below the previous field reads unambiguously as belonging to the input below it.

shortDef: Elements that look alike are perceived as belonging together.
longDef: Shared shape, size, colour or typographic treatment implies a shared role. It is why every link in a page should look like every other link, and why making one button visually distinct is enough to mark it as different in kind. Inconsistent styling reads as meaningful difference even when none was intended.
example: Underlined blue text is read as a link wherever it appears, so styling a heading that way makes people try to tap it.
misuse: Similar-looking elements that behave differently are worse than inconsistent ones, because the visual promise is broken.

shortDef: Elements inside a shared boundary are seen as one group.
longDef: A border, a background panel or a card draws a region, and everything inside it is read as a unit — strongly enough to override proximity. That makes cards a blunt but reliable grouping device. Overused, the page becomes a set of boxes with no hierarchy between them.
example: Two form fields inside a bordered panel read as one section even when a third field sits closer to them on the page.

shortDef: People complete incomplete shapes into whole familiar forms.
longDef: Given a partial outline, perception fills in the missing parts rather than seeing fragments. Logos and icons rely on it, and so does a carousel that shows a sliced card at the edge to imply more content. The implied whole must be obvious, or the result reads as broken rather than continuing.
example: A horizontal list that cuts the fifth card in half tells you there is more to scroll without needing an arrow.

shortDef: People read complex images in the simplest form available.
longDef: Perception resolves ambiguity toward the simplest, most stable interpretation, because that takes the least effort. Layouts built on regular shapes and consistent alignment are therefore processed faster and remembered better. Complex arrangements are not just harder to like — they are literally harder to see.
example: A grid of aligned rectangles is understood at a glance; the same content in overlapping irregular shapes has to be studied.

shortDef: The eye separates a subject from its background automatically.
longDef: Perception assigns one region as the object of attention and the rest as backdrop, using contrast, size and overlap to decide. Modals, dropdowns and focused states all depend on the separation being unmistakable. When figure and ground are too close in value, the interface feels flat and nothing seems clickable.
example: A dialog over a dimmed page reads instantly as the thing to deal with; the same dialog with no scrim competes with the content.

shortDef: The mental effort an interface demands to be used.
longDef: Load comes from three places: the inherent difficulty of the task, effort wasted on the interface itself, and effort spent actually learning. Design work is mostly about removing the second kind — unclear labels, remembered values, unnecessary decisions — so the available attention goes to the real task. It is finite and shared with whatever else the person is doing.
example: Showing the delivery address on the payment step removes the need to remember what was entered two screens ago.
misuse: "Reduce cognitive load" is not the same as "hide things". Hiding a needed control usually increases it.

shortDef: Grouping information into units that are easier to hold.
longDef: Breaking a long string or list into meaningful groups lets working memory treat each group as one item. It applies to numbers, to form sections and to navigation. The grouping has to match how people think about the content, or it adds a structure they then have to decode.
example: Sort codes shown as 20-30-40 are read back correctly far more often than 203040.

shortDef: What someone believes about how a system works.
longDef: People build an internal story of what the system is doing and predict its behaviour from it, whether or not that story matches the implementation. Trouble appears at the gap between the two — the user's model says the file is saved, the system's model says it is not. Research exists largely to find those gaps.
example: Many people believe deleting an email removes it permanently, which is why an unexpected "Trash" folder surprises them.
misuse: Not the same as the conceptual model the designer intends. The mental model is whatever the user actually ended up with.

shortDef: What an object makes possible for the person using it.
longDef: An affordance is a relationship between a thing and someone who can act on it: a handle affords pulling, a flat plate affords pushing. In screen design the relevant version is the perceived affordance — whether the person can tell the action is available. Something can afford tapping and still fail, if nothing signals it.
example: A raised, rounded rectangle with a label reads as pressable; the same words as plain grey text do not.
misuse: Often used to mean the visual cue itself. The cue is the signifier; the affordance is the possibility of the action.

shortDef: The cue that advertises an available action.
longDef: Signifiers are the marks that tell someone what to do: an underline, a chevron, a shadow, the word "Menu". They exist for communication, and they are what design mostly manipulates, since the underlying affordance is often already there. Flat interfaces went wrong by removing signifiers while keeping the affordances.
example: The chevron on a list row signifies that tapping it opens something, even though the whole row was always tappable.
misuse: Not interchangeable with affordance. A door still affords pushing when the "PUSH" sticker falls off — you just cannot tell.

shortDef: A door whose design tells you to do the wrong thing.
longDef: A handle that says pull on a door that opens outward is the canonical example of a signifier contradicting the mechanism. The name has become shorthand for any control whose appearance misleads about its behaviour. The failure is the design's, not the person's — which is the whole point of the term.
example: A flat rectangle styled like a button that turns out to be a static label, next to a plain word that is the real action.

shortDef: How clearly controls correspond to the things they affect.
longDef: Natural mapping arranges controls in the same spatial pattern as what they control, so the relationship needs no label or memory. The classic failure is a hob where four knobs sit in a row and four burners sit in a square. On screen it shows up whenever a control sits far from the thing it changes.
example: Seat adjustment buttons shaped like a seat: push the top forward to tilt the backrest forward.

shortDef: A limit built in so the wrong action is impossible.
longDef: Constraints prevent errors rather than reporting them: a date picker that cannot offer the 30th of February, a plug that only fits one way. They can be physical, logical, semantic or cultural. Well-placed constraints remove whole classes of error message from the product.
example: Disabling past dates in a booking calendar stops the error before it happens rather than validating it afterwards.
misuse: Disabling a control without explaining why is a constraint that creates confusion. Say what would make it available.

shortDef: Telling the user what just happened and what the system is doing.
longDef: Every action needs an acknowledgement, in a form and at a speed that matches the action's weight. Immediate and small for a tap, explicit and persistent for a payment. Silence is read as failure, which is why people press submit twice.
example: A button that switches to "Saving…" and then "Saved" prevents the double-submit that a silent button invites.
misuse: A spinner is not feedback about outcome, only about activity. It still has to end in a result.

shortDef: The gap between the system's state and the user's understanding of it.
longDef: Norman describes two gulfs: execution, the distance between what someone wants to do and the actions available, and evaluation, the distance between what the system did and what they can tell about it. Feedback narrows the second; clear affordances and signifiers narrow the first. Most confusing interfaces are wide in one or both.
example: A sync icon that spins forever leaves a wide gulf of evaluation — the user cannot tell whether their work is safe.

shortDef: Showing options beats making people remember them.
longDef: Recognising something on screen is far easier than retrieving it from memory unprompted. Interfaces should keep needed information visible or one glance away, rather than requiring users to carry it between steps. It is the argument for visible menus over memorised commands, and for showing what was entered before asking to confirm it.
example: A search field that shows recent searches beneath it, rather than an empty box you must remember what to type into.
misuse: It does not mean showing everything at once. Showing options on demand still counts as recognition.

shortDef: Designing so the mistake cannot happen in the first place.
longDef: Better than a good error message is a design where the error is impossible or is caught before it costs anything. Constraints, sensible defaults, confirmation for irreversible actions and forgiving input formats all do this. Slips need protection; genuine mistakes need better understanding upstream.
example: Asking "delete 42 files?" before an irreversible action, and offering undo for a reversible one.
misuse: A confirmation dialog on every action trains people to dismiss them, which removes the protection you were buying.

shortDef: Ten broad rules of thumb for judging interface usability.
longDef: Ten principles — visibility of status, match with the real world, user control, consistency, error prevention, recognition over recall, flexibility, minimalist design, error recovery, and help — used as a checklist for expert review. They are deliberately general, which makes them a good lens and a poor specification. They identify candidate problems; testing confirms them.
example: Reviewing a checkout against all ten produces a list like "no visible progress" and "error message does not say how to fix it".
misuse: A heuristic evaluation is not a substitute for watching real users. Experts predict problems; they do not observe them.

shortDef: The same thing looks and behaves the same way everywhere.
longDef: Internal consistency means a pattern works identically across your own product; external consistency means it matches the platform and the wider convention. Both let learning transfer, which is why a design system is worth its overhead. Consistency loses to clarity when a situation genuinely differs — but the bar for declaring that is high.
example: A destructive action that is always the rightmost button, always red-labelled and always confirmed, in every flow.
misuse: Consistency is not uniformity. Forcing one component to serve two different jobs makes both worse.

shortDef: People ignore anything that looks like an advert.
longDef: Users learn the visual signature of promotional content — right rail, bright colours, a boxed area at the top — and stop seeing it, whether or not it is actually an ad. Genuine content styled that way disappears with it. The fix is to look like the content, not to shout louder.
example: An important account notice placed in a coloured box in the top right is missed by most users, including in eye-tracking studies.
misuse: Not caused by ads alone. Any repeated decorative block in a predictable slot earns the same treatment.

shortDef: Too many options can stop people choosing at all.
longDef: Beyond a certain point, additional options reduce the likelihood of any decision and lower satisfaction with the one made. The effect depends on how comparable the options are and how much the person knows about the domain. Good defaults, filtering and recommended picks restore the ability to decide without removing the range.
example: A menu of forty plans with one marked "most popular" converts better than the same forty presented flat.
misuse: Not a law that fewer is always better. Experts in a domain often want the full range visible.
